subtype: Approach: trying and falling and trying again [Action]
passage: At the community centre ground, Nirmal held the handlebars of a small red cycle. No training wheels, only Damini the coach nearby with folded arms. "Ready?" Nirmal pushed off, wobbled twice and toppled onto the grass. Up again. This time he went four pedals before the front wheel twisted. Again. Six pedals. Damini said nothing but nodded. After an hour his knees were scuffed and his shirt was green with grass, but he was smiling. "I think I felt it," he said. "The falling part isn't so scary now." The last try took him almost to the far fence.

qa.q: How many pedals did Nirmal manage on the second try?
What might Nirmal feel when saying the falling part is not so scary?
qa.a: Nirmal probably feels growing confidence and a little pride, because the scuffed knees did not stop the smile. 😊

qa.q: What alternative approach could Nirmal use to learn faster, and why?
qa.a: Nirmal could ask Damini to hold the seat for the first pedals or glide without pedals first. That would give balance practice with less fear.

qa.q: How might Damini see Nirmal's tries?
qa.a: Damini stood with folded arms and only nodded, so Damini seems to trust the practice and probably sees steady improvement.

grounding: A boy hops on a cycle without training wheels, wobbles and falls, and each try lets him balance a little longer while fear fades.

subtype: Approach: trying and falling and trying again [Action]
passage: From my balcony I watched Jagdish from the ground floor take his friend Baljeet's old cycle, the one with no training wheels, out to the colony lane on Sunday. First try: two pedals, a wobble, and he tipped sideways into the hedge. He got up, brushed his knee and walked the cycle back to the lamp post. The second try went a little further. On the fourth, he fell hard and sat on the kerb for a while, holding his knee. I couldn't tell if he was about to cry or just catching his breath. Baljeet shouted, "Again!" He got back on. By evening he was reaching the gate before putting a foot down. On Wednesday there was a plaster on the knee, and he was out again, riding past the gate.

qa.q: Where did Jagdish walk the cycle back to after the first fall?
qa.a: He walked the cycle back to the lamp post.

qa.q: What might Jagdish have been feeling when he sat on the kerb holding his knee?
qa.a: He may have been hurt and shaken, perhaps close to tears, though the neighbour could not be sure; getting back on shows he was determined too.

qa.q: What could make these repeated falls a little safer while he keeps practising?
qa.a: He could wear a helmet and knee pads and practise on grass, so each fall costs less while he still learns balance by trying again.

qa.q: How does the practice look to Baljeet?
qa.a: Baljeet seems to enjoy it and wants Jagdish to keep going, shouting "Again!" to push him back on the cycle.

grounding: It shows a boy on a cycle without training wheels falling and trying again, balancing a bit longer each time.

subtype: Approach: trying and falling and trying again [Action]
passage:
Friday: Arnab's cousin Nitin wheeled out the tall cycle. "No side wheels?" Arnab asked. "None." Arnab pushed off, pedalled three times and crashed into Nani's marigold pots. He sat in the soil, staring at his scraped palms.
Saturday: Palms taped up, Arnab tried again and again in the courtyard. Each time he counted how long before a foot hit the ground: two seconds, three, once five. He fell twice more and got up both times without a word.
Tuesday: The scabs were drying. He still gripped the handles too tightly at the start, but he rode the full length of the courtyard and turned without a foot down. Nitin clapped. Arnab said "Again," before anyone could ask.

qa.q: What did Arnab crash into on Friday?
qa.a: He crashed into Nani's marigold pots.

qa.q: What does Arnab counting the seconds on Saturday suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: He seems determined and curious to see progress, even though the falls must have stung and frightened him.

qa.q: What else could help Arnab if the falls start to put him off?
qa.a: He could lower the seat so his feet reach the ground, which makes each try less scary and lets him keep practising balance.

qa.q: How does Arnab's week of practice look to Nitin?
qa.a: Nitin sees Arnab go from crashing to turning smoothly, and is proud enough to clap on Tuesday.

grounding: It shows a boy riding without training wheels, falling and retrying over several days until he balances longer.
